title: Architecture Patterns
tagline: From monolith to microservices — the structural patterns that shape how systems are built, deployed, and scaled.

sections.content:
Architecture is the set of decisions that are hardest to change later. Not which library to use or which database column to add — but whether the system is one deployable unit or dozens, whether services call each other directly or through a broker, whether work happens synchronously or via a queue. Getting these wrong at scale means rewrites measured in engineer-years.

The stakes are high because architectural decisions embed themselves into team structure, deployment pipelines, monitoring strategy, and SLA guarantees. They constrain every future decision made on top of them. Conway's Law — that software architecture tends to mirror the communication structure of the organization building it — is not just an observation but a warning: change the architecture without changing the team structure and it will drift back.

The good news is that a small vocabulary of **patterns** covers 90 % of real production systems. **Client-server**, **layered (N-tier)**, **monolith vs. microservices**, **event-driven**, **API gateway**, **load balancing**, **CQRS**, and **service mesh** are the building blocks every senior engineer reasons in. These patterns are not fashions — many are decades old and will be in use decades from now. Master the problem each pattern solves, understand its costs, and you can evaluate any architecture diagram in minutes.

This chapter covers those patterns with rigor: what problem each solves, what the structure looks like, worked code examples, and critically — when **not** to use each one. Real systems are built from combinations of these patterns, and the skill is in choosing the right combination for the constraints at hand.

sections.title: Restaurant Kitchen Models
sections.content:
A **monolith** is a single open kitchen where every chef shares the same tools, stove, and pantry. Coordination is easy — chefs can hand dishes directly to each other — and the head chef can see everything happening at once. But one broken stove shuts the whole kitchen down, the kitchen cannot scale the pasta station without scaling everything else, and a fire in one corner threatens the whole restaurant.

**Microservices** are separate food stations — sushi, grill, pastry, salad — each with dedicated tools, storage, and staff. The head waiter (the **API gateway**) routes orders to the right station. A ticket rail (the **message queue**) lets the grill station fire a dessert order to pastry without waiting for it to finish; pastry picks up the ticket when ready. More moving parts, but a broken fryer only kills the fries; the sushi station keeps running.

The **load balancer** is a second head waiter who splits incoming diners across two identical dining rooms so neither gets overwhelmed. **CQRS** is the restaurant's separation of the kitchen (write path, complex prep) from the buffet display (read path, optimised presentation). Each pattern is a solution to a specific operational pain — and like kitchen design, the right layout depends on the volume and kind of cooking you expect to do.

sections.title: Client-Server: The Foundational Split
sections.content:
**Client-server** is the most fundamental architectural pattern. Clients initiate requests; servers fulfill them. The HTTP protocol formalized this split and it underlies every web application, mobile app, and API ever built.

The variant matters: a **thin client** puts all logic on the server and sends rendered HTML (traditional server-side rendering, PHP, Rails). A **thick client** (SPA + API) sends JSON and runs rendering logic in the browser. The choice changes where you deploy, where you cache, and where you scale.

A critical implication: the client-server boundary is a **trust boundary**. The server must validate every input as if the client is adversarial — because in production, some clients will be. Never rely on client-side validation alone. This is not paranoia; it is the architectural consequence of running code on a machine you do not control.

Client-server also implies **statelessness** in the purest REST model: each request carries all the context the server needs. Session state is stored server-side (in a database or Redis) or encoded in a signed token (JWT) sent with every request. Stateless servers are much easier to scale horizontally — add more instances, and any instance can handle any request.

sections.title: Layered (N-Tier) Architecture: Separation of Concerns
sections.content:
The **layered architecture** (also called N-tier) organises a codebase into horizontal layers where each layer only talks to the layer directly below it. The classic three layers are:

1. **Presentation layer** — handles HTTP requests, validates input, serialises responses. In a NestJS or Express app this is your controllers and route handlers.
2. **Business logic layer** — implements domain rules, orchestrates workflows, enforces invariants. This is your service classes. It has no knowledge of HTTP or the database driver.
3. **Data access layer** — talks to the database, translates between domain objects and DB rows. This is your repositories, ORM models, or raw query functions.

The rule: **dependencies flow downward only**. The controller calls the service; the service calls the repository. The repository never calls the service; the service never builds an HTTP response. This discipline makes each layer independently testable — you can test the service by mocking the repository, without spinning up a database.

Layered architecture is the default inside a monolith. Its failure mode is the **big ball of mud**: over time, developers take shortcuts, controllers call repositories directly, services build HTML, and layers blur. Enforce the boundaries through code review, linting rules (`no-restricted-imports`), or module boundaries.

A common extension is the **hexagonal architecture** (ports and adapters): define interfaces (ports) that the domain core depends on, and swap concrete implementations (adapters) — a real Postgres adapter in production, an in-memory adapter in tests. This is especially powerful when you need to migrate databases or add a second transport (HTTP + gRPC + CLI) without touching domain logic.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A["HTTP Request"] --> B["Controller Layer\n(validation, routing)"]
  B --> C["Service Layer\n(business logic)"]
  C --> D["Repository Layer\n(data access)"]
  D --> E["Database\n(Postgres / Redis)"]
  C --> F["External APIs\n(payment, email)"]
  B --> G["HTTP Response\n(serialised JSON)"]
sections.caption: Layered architecture: dependencies flow downward. The service layer owns business logic and never imports HTTP primitives; the controller never queries the database directly.

sections.title: Monolith vs. Microservices: The Most Consequential Decision
sections.content:
No architectural decision generates more debate or more conference talks. Let us be precise about what each means and what you actually trade.

**A monolith** is a single deployable unit. All modules — auth, orders, products, notifications — are compiled and deployed together. They run in the same process, share the same memory heap, and typically share the same database. Function calls between modules are in-process and near-free. You deploy by shipping one artefact. You debug with one set of logs. You develop by running one server.

**Microservices** decompose the system by **business domain**. Each service is an independently deployable process that owns its own data store and exposes an API. The order service has its own Postgres schema; the notification service has its own Redis; they communicate over the network via HTTP, gRPC, or message queues.

The **advantages of microservices** are real:
- **Independent deployability**: the notification team deploys without touching the order team's codebase.
- **Independent scalability**: scale the image-processing service to 50 instances without wasting resources on the auth service.
- **Technology heterogeneity**: the recommendation engine can be Python + NumPy; the rest of the system can be Node.js.
- **Fault isolation**: a memory leak in the notification service crashes that service, not the order service.

The **costs are equally real**:
- **Network latency and partial failure**: an in-process call takes microseconds; an HTTP call to another service takes milliseconds and can fail, time out, or return a 503.
- **Distributed tracing**: a bug that spans three services requires correlating logs from three separate log streams with a shared trace ID.
- **Eventual consistency**: the orders DB says an order exists; the notifications DB, replicated asynchronously, may not yet know. Your code must reason about this lag.
- **Operational overhead**: each service needs its own CI/CD pipeline, health checks, Kubernetes deployment manifest, alerting rules, and on-call rotation.
- **Testing complexity**: integration testing across services requires running multiple services simultaneously.

The industry consensus, backed by practitioners at Amazon, Netflix, and Shopify (all of whom started monolithic): **start monolith, extract microservices when the pain is real and measurable**. The seams where extraction makes sense reveal themselves when you have a module that is a deployment bottleneck, a scaling outlier, or a team coordination chokepoint. Extract then — not before.

flowchart LR

sections.caption: Monolith: one process, shared database, in-process calls. Microservices: separate processes, separate databases, network calls — independent deployability at the cost of distributed systems complexity.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The gateway handles auth and rate limiting once, then proxies to the correct microservice. Downstream services trust the `x-user-id` header injected by the gateway and never touch a JWT themselves — a clean separation of cross-cutting infrastructure from domain logic. The `x-request-id` header enables distributed tracing: every log line in every service records this ID, so you can reconstruct the full call chain.

sections.title: API Gateway: The System's Front Door
sections.content:
An **API gateway** is the single entry point for all client traffic. Rather than exposing each microservice on a public port, all requests enter through the gateway, which handles **cross-cutting concerns** — responsibilities that every service would otherwise need to implement independently.

Typical gateway responsibilities:
- **Authentication and authorisation**: verify JWT or session token, inject user identity as a trusted internal header
- **Rate limiting and throttling**: prevent abuse; enforce per-client and per-endpoint quotas
- **SSL/TLS termination**: decrypt HTTPS at the gateway; traffic inside the private network can be plain HTTP, reducing per-service TLS overhead
- **Request routing**: map URL paths (or subdomains) to backend services
- **Request/response transformation**: rename headers, reshape JSON, translate REST to gRPC
- **Observability**: emit a request log and trace span for every request before it reaches a service
- **Canary routing**: send 5 % of traffic to the new version of a service for A/B testing

Popular production gateways: **Kong** (open source, Nginx-based), **AWS API Gateway** (managed, integrates with Lambda and ECS), **Nginx / Caddy** (reverse proxy with gateway features), **Envoy** (often used as the data plane in service meshes).

A common mistake is putting **business logic** in the gateway. If the gateway starts knowing about orders, discounts, or customer tiers, it becomes a source of coupling and a deployment bottleneck. The gateway should be dumb infrastructure that knows about HTTP, not about your domain.

sections.title: Load Balancing: Horizontal Scalability and Failover
sections.content:
A **load balancer** sits in front of multiple identical instances of the same service and distributes incoming requests across them. The purpose is twofold: **horizontal scaling** (add more instances to handle more traffic) and **automatic failover** (stop sending traffic to an unhealthy instance).

Load balancing algorithms:
- **Round robin**: requests rotate through instances in order. Simple and effective when requests are roughly equal in cost.
- **Least connections**: route to the instance with the fewest active connections. Better when requests vary in duration (e.g., a mix of quick queries and long uploads).
- **IP hash / sticky sessions**: always route the same client IP to the same instance. Required when session state is stored locally on the instance (though stateless design is far preferable).
- **Weighted round robin**: send more traffic to larger or faster instances.

**Health checks** are fundamental: the load balancer periodically sends a probe (usually `GET /health`) to each instance. If an instance fails two consecutive checks, it is removed from the rotation until it recovers. This is how rolling deployments work safely — bring up a new instance, wait for it to pass health checks, then drain the old one.

Load balancers operate at different OSI layers:
- **Layer 4 (TCP)**: routes based on IP and port, does not inspect HTTP. Ultra-low latency. AWS NLB.
- **Layer 7 (HTTP)**: inspects URLs, headers, and cookies; can do path-based routing, cookie-based affinity, and SSL termination. AWS ALB, Nginx, HAProxy.

For most web services, Layer 7 is the right choice — the ability to do path-based routing (`/api/` → API cluster, `/static/` → S3) and header-based canary releases is worth the small latency overhead.

sections.title: Message Queues and Event-Driven Architecture
sections.content:
A **message queue** (or message broker) decouples producers from consumers by introducing an intermediary that stores messages until consumers are ready to process them. The producer publishes a message and continues; it does not wait for the consumer to acknowledge. This is **temporal decoupling**.

Core concepts:
- **Producer**: the service that publishes messages (the order service publishes `order.created`).
- **Queue / Topic**: the durable buffer where messages are stored. A **queue** typically delivers each message to one consumer. A **topic** (Kafka, SNS) delivers each message to all subscribers — useful for fan-out.
- **Consumer**: the service that pulls or receives messages and processes them. Multiple consumers can process in parallel, providing horizontal scaling of async work.
- **Acknowledgement (ack)**: the consumer signals successful processing; the broker removes the message. If the consumer crashes before acking, the broker redelivers — **at-least-once delivery**.

Why this matters architecturally:
1. **Resilience**: if the notification service is down, messages queue up and are delivered when it recovers. The order service never sees the failure.
2. **Traffic buffering**: a sudden spike of 10,000 orders publishes 10,000 events to the queue. The email service processes them at its own pace — say, 500/second — instead of being overwhelmed or requiring the same scaling capacity as the order service.
3. **Fan-out**: a single `order.created` event is consumed independently by notifications, fulfillment, analytics, and fraud detection — without the order service knowing these consumers exist.
4. **Audit log**: Kafka retains messages for days or weeks. You can replay historical events to rebuild a view or bootstrap a new service.

Popular brokers:
- **RabbitMQ**: traditional message queue, AMQP protocol, excellent for task queues and RPC patterns.
- **Apache Kafka**: high-throughput distributed log, event streaming, retained messages, consumer groups. The choice for event sourcing and streaming analytics.
- **AWS SQS + SNS**: managed, zero ops, good for simple fan-out patterns in AWS.
- **Redis Streams**: lightweight, low-latency, good for in-process fan-out when full Kafka overhead is not warranted.

The most common pitfall is **not handling idempotency**. With at-least-once delivery, a consumer may process the same message twice (due to a network blip before the ack). Every consumer must be idempotent: processing the same message twice should produce the same result as processing it once. Store a processed event ID in the database and skip duplicates.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The producer publishes after writing to the database — never before, to avoid publishing an event for a transaction that will be rolled back. The consumer records processed event IDs before acking, making duplicate delivery harmless. The nack on failure triggers redelivery with backoff — the broker acts as a retry mechanism without the producer needing to know.

sections.title: CQRS: Separating Reads from Writes
sections.content:
**CQRS** (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) is the pattern of using **different models for writing data** (commands) **and reading data** (queries). The insight: write models need to enforce invariants and business rules (complex, transactional); read models need to return data in shapes optimised for UI display (simple, denormalised, fast).

In a naive system, the same Postgres table serves both. An order insert must lock rows and validate business rules; the order-list page wants a denormalised join of orders, customer names, and product titles — an expensive query run on every page load. CQRS separates these:

- **Write side**: the `OrderService.createOrder()` command validates, saves normalised rows, and publishes an `order.created` event.
- **Read side**: an event consumer listens to `order.created` and writes a pre-computed, denormalised record to a **read store** (could be the same Postgres DB in a separate table, or Elasticsearch, or Redis). The read store is shaped exactly for the UI's query.
- **Query side**: the `OrderQueryService.listOrders()` reads from the read store — no joins, no heavy computation, just a simple index scan.

The cost: **eventual consistency**. There is a small lag between a write completing and the read store reflecting it. For many UIs this is acceptable (show a spinner, poll briefly). For banking or inventory, it may not be.

CQRS is often combined with **Event Sourcing**: instead of storing the current state of an entity, store every event that led to that state (`order.created`, `order.item_added`, `order.shipped`). The current state is the fold of all events. This gives a perfect audit log and the ability to replay history to build new projections. The complexity cost is significant — use Event Sourcing only when audit trails or temporal queries are genuine requirements.

Real frameworks using CQRS: **Axon Framework** (Java), **MediatR** (C#/.NET), **NestJS CQRS module**. It is also the architectural backbone of most React state managers — dispatching actions (commands) updates a store (write side) from which selectors (read side) derive derived data.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Client"] --> B["Command Handler\n(write model)"]
  B --> C["Write Store\n(normalised DB)"]
  B --> D["Event Bus"]
  D --> E["Projection Handler\n(read model builder)"]
  E --> F["Read Store\n(denormalised / search)"]
  A --> G["Query Handler\n(read model)"]
  G --> F
sections.caption: CQRS flow: commands write to the normalised store and emit events. A projection handler builds the read store from those events. Queries hit the read store only — no joins, no locks.

sections.title: Service Mesh: Infrastructure for Microservice Communication
sections.content:
As microservices proliferate, a new class of problems emerges: every service-to-service call needs **mutual TLS** (mTLS) for encryption and authentication, **retry logic** with exponential backoff, **circuit breaking** to stop calling a failing service, **timeout enforcement**, and **distributed tracing** header propagation. If each service implements these in its application code, the implementations diverge, bugs accumulate, and every new service starts with a huge boilerplate burden.

A **service mesh** externalises this into infrastructure by deploying a **sidecar proxy** (typically Envoy) alongside each service container. All inter-service traffic flows through the sidecar, which handles mTLS, retries, circuit breaking, load balancing, and telemetry — transparently, without application code changes.

Key components:
- **Data plane**: the sidecar proxies (Envoy instances) that handle actual traffic. They are deployed in every pod.
- **Control plane**: the central system (Istio Pilot, Linkerd Controller) that pushes configuration to all sidecars — 'apply these retry rules to calls from orders-service to payment-service'.
- **Traffic policies**: define timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, traffic splits (canary), and rate limits declaratively in YAML, applied mesh-wide.

The **circuit breaker** pattern deserves special attention. When a downstream service starts failing, a naive retry loop hammers it further, causing a cascading failure. A circuit breaker tracks failure rate; when it exceeds a threshold, the circuit 'opens' and all calls fail immediately (fast fail) for a cooldown period, giving the downstream service space to recover. After the cooldown, the circuit is 'half-open' — one request is allowed through as a probe. If it succeeds, the circuit closes. If not, the cooldown resets.

Service meshes (Istio, Linkerd, Consul Connect) add significant operational complexity. They are worth the investment at 20+ microservices with sophisticated traffic management needs. For smaller deployments, implementing retries and circuit breaking in each service via a library (axios-retry, opossum, Resilience4j) is simpler and sufficient.

sections.mermaid:
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Closed
  Closed --> Open: "failure rate > threshold"
  Open --> HalfOpen: "cooldown expires"
  HalfOpen --> Closed: "probe request succeeds"
  HalfOpen --> Open: "probe request fails"
sections.caption: Circuit breaker state machine: Closed (normal operation) → Open (fail fast on errors) → Half-Open (test probe) → back to Closed on success. This prevents cascading failures when a downstream service degrades.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The circuit breaker wraps any async call. After 3 consecutive failures it opens and fast-fails for 5 seconds — no network calls are made during the cooldown. The caller handles the open-circuit error gracefully by queueing the payment rather than returning a 500 to the end user. This is the **graceful degradation** pattern: the system provides a reduced-quality response rather than failing completely.

sections.content: **Real-world pattern combinations**: Netflix's architecture uses all of these simultaneously. An API gateway (Zuul/Spring Cloud Gateway) handles routing and auth. A load balancer (ELB) distributes across gateway instances. Behind the gateway, hundreds of microservices communicate via Eureka (service discovery) and Hystrix (circuit breaking). Kafka carries events between services. A service mesh (moving toward Envoy) handles mTLS. CQRS is used for the recommendation engine — writes go to a graph store, reads come from a pre-computed Cassandra table. No single pattern is the whole answer; they compose.

**When NOT to use microservices**: if your team has fewer than 20 engineers, if you don't have a mature DevOps / platform team, if your product hasn't found product-market fit yet (the domain model will change dramatically), or if you can't afford the operational overhead of distributed tracing, multi-service deployments, and on-call rotations across services. Shopify ran on a Rails monolith for over a decade and at one point processed more commerce volume than Amazon.com. A well-organised monolith with clear module boundaries is not a failure — it is often the right engineering decision. Microservices are an organisational pattern as much as a technical one: they make sense when teams need to deploy independently and own their services end-to-end.

items: **Client-server** is the foundational split: clients request, servers respond. The trust boundary means the server always validates inputs regardless of client-side validation.
**Layered architecture** separates presentation, business logic, and data access; dependencies flow downward only — controllers call services, services call repositories, never the reverse.

**Monolith** is simpler to build, test, and debug; start here. **Microservices** give independent deployability and scaling at the real cost of distributed systems complexity — network failures, eventual consistency, and operational overhead.
**API gateway** centralises cross-cutting concerns (auth, rate limiting, SSL termination, routing) so individual services remain focused on domain logic and never re-implement infrastructure.

**Message queues** decouple producers from consumers temporally: the producer publishes and moves on; consumers process at their own pace. Consumers must be **idempotent** because at-least-once delivery is the norm.
**CQRS** separates write models (enforce invariants, normalised) from read models (denormalised, UI-shaped) — enabling independently scalable read and write paths at the cost of eventual consistency.

**Circuit breakers** prevent cascading failures by fast-failing calls to a struggling downstream service during a cooldown period, giving it space to recover — a critical resilience pattern in any microservices system.

quiz.question: What is the primary advantage of an API gateway over having clients call microservices directly?
options: It makes every request faster by caching all responses in memory
It centralises cross-cutting concerns like auth, rate limiting, and routing in one place
It eliminates the need for a load balancer entirely
It automatically converts REST endpoints to GraphQL
quiz.explanation: Without a gateway, every service must independently implement auth, rate limiting, SSL termination, and observability. The gateway handles these once for all services, keeping services focused on domain logic and avoiding duplicated infrastructure code.

quiz.question: A message queue decouples services primarily by providing:
options: A shared database both producer and consumer can query
Synchronous RPC with automatic retry on failure
Temporal decoupling — the producer publishes and continues without waiting for the consumer
A binary protocol that is faster than HTTP
quiz.explanation: The core value of a message queue is temporal decoupling: the producer publishes and moves on. The consumer processes the event when it is ready, at its own pace, and can even be offline when the event is published — the broker holds the message until delivery is possible.

quiz.question: Why must message queue consumers be idempotent?
options: Consumers run in parallel and share state
Message brokers guarantee exactly-once delivery
At-least-once delivery means the same message may be delivered more than once
Producers always publish duplicate events for redundancy
quiz.explanation: Most message brokers guarantee at-least-once delivery: if a consumer crashes after processing but before acking, the broker redelivers the message. A consumer that sends two emails for one order is a bug. Idempotency — checking a processed-event log — makes duplicate delivery harmless.

quiz.question: In layered architecture, which direction do dependencies flow?
options: Upward — repositories call services, services call controllers
Bidirectional — any layer can call any other layer
Downward — controllers call services, services call repositories
Horizontal — layers at the same level share logic freely
quiz.explanation: In layered architecture, dependencies flow strictly downward: the presentation layer calls the service layer, which calls the data access layer. The data access layer never imports from the service layer. This one-way dependency makes each layer independently testable.

quiz.question: What does a circuit breaker do when it transitions to the OPEN state?
options: It retries the failed call with exponential backoff
It fast-fails all calls immediately without making network requests to the downstream service
It routes traffic to a backup service automatically
It sends an alert to on-call engineers and waits for manual intervention
quiz.explanation: When the circuit opens (due to exceeding the failure threshold), all subsequent calls fail immediately — no network requests are made. This gives the downstream service space to recover and prevents cascading failures caused by a thundering herd of retries.

quiz.question: What does it mean for microservices to follow the 'database per service' pattern?
options: Every service instance gets its own database replica for low latency
Each service has its own dedicated database; other services access its data through the service's API, not direct DB queries
Services share one database but use separate schemas and tables
A central data warehouse aggregates all service databases nightly
quiz.explanation: Database per service means no direct cross-service database queries. Service B must call Service A's API to read A's data. This enforces loose coupling — Service A can change its schema, migrate databases, or restructure its tables without breaking Service B.

quiz.question: In CQRS, what is the primary reason for maintaining a separate read model (read store)?
options: To comply with GDPR data isolation requirements
To avoid any eventual consistency in the system
To serve queries in shapes optimised for the UI without complex joins on the write store
To store historical audit logs of every state change
quiz.explanation: The write store is normalised for correctness and transactional integrity. The read store is denormalised, pre-computed, and shaped exactly for UI queries — avoiding expensive joins on every page load. The tradeoff is eventual consistency between the write and read stores.

quiz.question: What is the 'thundering herd' problem in microservices and which pattern prevents it?
options: Too many services deploying simultaneously — prevented by blue-green deployments
All retries hitting a recovering service simultaneously — prevented by circuit breakers with exponential backoff
A load balancer sending all traffic to one instance — prevented by round-robin routing
Multiple consumers racing to read the same queue message — prevented by consumer groups
quiz.explanation: When a downstream service recovers after an outage, all queued retries from upstream services hit it at once — potentially overwhelming it again. Circuit breakers with exponential backoff and jitter spread the retry load over time, giving the recovering service a chance to stabilise.

quiz.question: A Layer 7 load balancer differs from a Layer 4 load balancer in that it:
options: Operates at 7x the throughput of a Layer 4 load balancer
Can inspect HTTP headers and URLs to make routing decisions, enabling path-based routing and canary releases
Only works with HTTPS traffic, not plain HTTP
Handles database connection pooling in addition to HTTP routing
quiz.explanation: Layer 4 load balancers route based on TCP/IP information (IP address and port) without inspecting application-layer content. Layer 7 load balancers inspect HTTP headers, URLs, and cookies — enabling path-based routing (/api/ → one cluster, /static/ → another) and header-based canary releases.

quiz.question: Which of the following is a strong signal that a monolith should extract a specific module as a microservice?
options: The codebase has more than 50,000 lines of code
The team has been using the monolith for more than two years
A specific module is a deployment bottleneck, scaling outlier, or team coordination chokepoint
The product has found product-market fit and is growing
quiz.explanation: The right time to extract a service is when concrete pain exists: a module that blocks all deployments (deployment bottleneck), one that needs 10x more resources than the rest (scaling outlier), or one owned by a team whose changes constantly conflict with others (coordination chokepoint). Growth and code size alone are not sufficient reasons.
